doc.title: Rick Montalbano interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, August 12, 2011

title: Wrong notes: Miles, Jack Palmer and being in the moment
summary: Asked about wrong notes, he prefers 'better choices'. He recounts Palmer's dislike of Miles's sound and says any note can work if you stay in the moment.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: That’s really interesting you say that because I was sort of trying to phrase a question I’ve been asking recently this question that has to do with wrong notes when you’re improvising.

Wrong notes. Or are there any wrong notes? And when I think of Miles especially, and I listen to Miles, sometimes he plays these notes like where’d that come from? Did he do that on purpose? Was it a cracked note but because it’s Miles it’s okay? I mean when you play or when you teach your students, do you ever sort of deal with the idea of right and wrong notes?

I try to phrase it as better choices. In Miles’ case, I mean he did crack. A lot of people didn’t listen to him. I can remember trumpet players — Jack Palmer. Jack Palmer loved what he played and he hated his sound. He used to say “ah Miles Davis, you might as well be playing with a comb and wax paper, you know. That’s what it sounded like, and especially when he put the Harmon in. You know. But I can’t imagine that he — the thing is with, if you’re calling them wrong notes, I guess anything, if you put it in the proper context you can make virtually anything from the chromatic scale work. Any note can work over something if it’s played the right way and I think if its enough in the moment to deal with the sound you just made and make it work somehow you know. Early on you know — I’m sure you remember this — it was that if you played something you’d play it again, as if you did — but that’s kind of, I think, a little superficial. But I think the idea of being enough in the moment helps in that regard to take a particular © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -9-

sound that maybe initially is a rub against the chord and kind of work your way back in or whatever. So it has a lot to do with that thing of being in it, which is the cause of a lot of frustration sometimes. I mean that to me is the single most important thing, in my case at least, being able to filter everything out and be in the now. I know it sounds a little corny but you know what I’m saying.
